sections.headline: Most delivery problems are definition problems.
sections.body: Four and a half years turning stakeholder noise into requirements, roadmaps and dashboards people actually use — as a business analyst at Codewalla, then Senior Associate in analytics at WNS. Now reading for a PGCM at Great Lakes, still chasing the same thing: the problem underneath the problem.

sections.title: Three I would defend in an interview
Agree on it before you build it
sections.body: Every project I have run starts the same way: the problem in a sentence, whose problem it is, what we are not doing, and the one number that will tell us we were right. It is unglamorous and it is most of the job. When a team is arguing in week six, it is usually because nobody wrote that down in week one.

items.title: Ask the people doing the workaround
items.note: Ops leads and analysts already know where the process leaks. Requirements written from the real routine, not the documented one, survive contact with delivery.

items.title: Let the story carry its acceptance criteria
items.note: Most rework I have seen came from a story that read clearly and meant three different things. Rework fell 20% once each one had to say how it would be checked.

items.title: Settle the definitions, then the dashboard
items.note: Agreeing what a KPI counts is the argument worth having. Build the chart first and you have automated a disagreement.

sections.title: If you are hiring someone to ask the awkward question early, write to me.

projects.title: The allocation app nobody had to be told to use
projects.summary: Chat-and-spreadsheet allocation replaced by one shared view, specced from the real handoff. 95% adoption, rework down 20%.
projects.intro: An internal product that replaced chat-and-spreadsheet task allocation with one shared view — specced from the real handoff rather than the documented process, and adopted without a mandate.
projects.objective: Give every team one trustworthy view of who holds what, so that allocation stops being reconstructed by hand each morning. The brief asked for a manager's tracker; the objective I wrote instead was shared visibility, because a tool only managers opened would have become a sixth version of the truth.
did: Sat on both sides of the handoff for a week and wrote the requirements against what people actually did — including the workarounds nobody had documented.

Held the product roadmap and a prioritised backlog with the development team, every user story carrying its own acceptance criteria. Where a story could be read two ways it was split, not clarified in a comment.
Rolled out team by team rather than all at once, so each group's objections arrived while there was still room to act on them.
projects.resultText: Adoption held without a mandate, which is the number I am actually proud of. Rework fell once acceptance criteria travelled with the story instead of living in a conversation.
projects.conclusion: The build was never the hard part. What made it stick was refusing the brief's framing early enough that it cost a conversation rather than a quarter. If I ran it again I would fix the success metric in the same document as the scope.

projects.title: Retiring the Monday-morning spreadsheet
projects.summary: KPI definitions settled first, then dashboards built around the decisions they serve. 80% of the manual analysis automated.
projects.intro: A KPI and reporting layer for leadership, built after the definitions were settled rather than before — which is why the fortnightly argument about whose number was right did not come back.
projects.objective: Give leadership numbers they can act on the day they are produced. The brief was to automate the weekly report; the objective I wrote was to make the reporting trustworthy first, because two teams were reporting the same KPI with different definitions and both were defensible.
did: Ran the definitions to ground first: one page per KPI stating what it counts, what it excludes, and which decision it exists to support. Anything no decision needed was cut from the report.
Built the dashboards around those decisions rather than around the data we happened to hold, and automated the collection so no analyst assembled a figure by hand.
Left the drill-downs open so operations could interrogate a number without routing the question through me.
projects.resultText: Leadership stopped reading last week's numbers, and the recurring dispute over whose figure was correct disappeared with the definitions document.
projects.conclusion: Automation was the easy half. Agreeing what a number means is what decides whether anyone trusts the chart. I did build more views than were needed — two of six went unopened after the first month — and would now ship three and wait to be asked.

projects.title: Gaming Arena: pricing a venture in three days
projects.summary: Pricing experiments and hourly competitor reads mapped demand instead of guessing at it. Sustained profitability within three days.
projects.intro: A live economics simulation run as a real venture: pricing experiments and hourly competitor reads instead of matching whatever the neighbouring stall charged.
projects.objective: Reach sustained profitability inside a three-day simulation without knowing the demand curve in advance — and come out of it able to point at what customers would actually pay, rather than at a hunch that happened to work.
did: Treated day one as measurement rather than trading: deliberate price moves at both ends of the range to find where demand bent.
Tracked competitor pricing hourly and held our position when they undercut, on the read that their volume would not cover the cut.
Reset the price once a day at most, so each move could be attributed to something rather than lost in noise.
projects.resultText: Profitability held for the rest of the simulation, and we finished with a demand curve I could show rather than describe.
projects.conclusion: Spending the first day learning instead of earning felt expensive and was not. The one real failure was record-keeping: the experiments were logged unevenly, so part of what we learned stayed in memory.
